```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ me { __typename email drafts { title } } }"
export const Viewer = builder.drizzleInterface('users', {
  variant: 'Viewer',
  select: { columns: { id: true, role: true } },
  resolveType: (user) => (user.role === 'editor' ? 'EditorViewer' : 'AuthorViewer'),
  fields: (t) => ({
    user: t.variant('users'),
    email: t.exposeString('email'),
    drafts: t.relation('posts', {
      query: { where: { published: false }, orderBy: { id: 'asc' } },
    }),
  }),
});
```

`resolveType` uses the selected `role` discriminator and returns GraphQL type names. Returning
names avoids a circular reference between the interface and its implementations.

## Selecting a viewer implementation [#selecting-a-viewer-implementation]

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ me { __typename drafts { title } ... on EditorViewer { canReviewSubmissions } } }"
builder.drizzleObject('users', {
  variant: 'EditorViewer',
  interfaces: [Viewer],
  select: { columns: { id: true, role: true } },
  fields: (t) => ({ canReviewSubmissions: t.boolean({ resolve: () => true }) }),
});
builder.drizzleObject('users', {
  variant: 'AuthorViewer',
  interfaces: [Viewer],
  select: { columns: { id: true, role: true } },
});
```

The interface's `select` is planned whenever a field returns the interface. An implementation's
own selection is planned when a fragment narrows to it. Selections are not inherited; put data
required by an implementation in its selection as well. An implementation may select additional
columns or expressions for fields that do not belong on the interface.

Maya (`userId: 1`) resolves to EditorViewer with `canReviewSubmissions: true`. Leo (`userId: 2`)
resolves to AuthorViewer, so the editor fragment contributes no field. The interface describes
those result shapes; the authenticated root lookup enforces whose drafts are returned.

## Extending an interface [#extending-an-interface]

Fields can be added to an interface later with `builder.drizzleInterfaceField` and
`builder.drizzleInterfaceFields`, which take the interface ref (or the table name) like their
`drizzleObjectField(s)` counterparts:

```ts
builder.drizzleInterfaceFields(Viewer, (t) => ({
  publishedPosts: t.relatedConnection('posts', {
    query: { where: { published: true } },
  }),
}));
```

An object type implementing a drizzle interface must be based on the same table. A plain object
type that implements one is planned with the interface's table, so fragments on it will select the
relations it inherits.


# Drizzle Objects
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/objects
Defining GraphQL object types based on drizzle tables


Use the [configured builder](./setup) to map a Drizzle table to a GraphQL type. Defining a type
registers its fields; a root lookup makes them queryable.

## Defining Objects [#defining-objects]

The `builder.drizzleObject` method can be used to define GraphQL Object types based on a drizzle
table:

```ts
const User = builder.drizzleObject('users', {
  name: 'User',
  fields: (t) => ({
    firstName: t.exposeString('firstName'),
    lastName: t.exposeString('lastName'),
  }),
});
```

You will be able to "expose" any column in the table, and GraphQL fields do not need to match the
names of the columns in your database. The returned `User` can be used like any other `ObjectRef`
in Pothos.

The example uses `builder.drizzleNode`, which adds a Relay ID and node refetching to the
same object API. See [Relay](./relay) for node IDs and refetching.

## Custom fields [#custom-fields]

A GraphQL field can combine several columns. The author’s full name declares both columns in
its selection and computes the string from the loaded row:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ author(id: 1) { fullName } }"
fullName: t.string({
  select: { columns: { firstName: true, lastName: true } },
  resolve: (user) => `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`,
}),
```

This field belongs in User's `fields` callback. With the default type selection, all scalar
columns are available; with `select: {}`, computed fields must declare what they read.
[Selections](./selections) explains when those columns and relations are loaded.

## Drizzle Fields [#drizzle-fields]

`t.drizzleField` can return a Drizzle object from Query or from any other object type. Its
resolver receives a `query` function before the usual resolver arguments. Call that function and
pass its result to `findFirst` or `findMany`: it merges your filters and ordering with the
requirements of the GraphQL selection.

### A nullable author lookup [#a-nullable-author-lookup]

The author page accepts an integer ID. A missing author returns null, matching the result of
`findFirst` and the field's `nullable: true` option:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle"
builder.queryType({
  fields: (t) => ({
    author: t.drizzleField({
      type: 'users',
      nullable: true,
      args: { id: t.arg.int({ required: true }) },
      resolve: (query, _root, args) => {
        return db.query.users.findFirst(
          query({
            where: { id: args.id },
          }),
        );
      },
    }),
  }),
});
```

`author(id: 1) { fullName }` returns Maya Chen. `author(id: 999) { fullName }` returns null.
Adding `posts { title }` loads the public posts through the same root resolver.

For a list field, use `type: ['users']` and `db.query.users.findMany(query())`. A plain lookup
without arguments can pass no options to `query`; fields with filters pass those options to it.
If the `with` you pass to `query` names a relation the type's `select` also loads, the arguments
from the type's `select` are used for that relation.

### `drizzleFieldWithInput` [#drizzlefieldwithinput]

With the [with-input plugin](https://pothos-graphql.dev/docs/plugins/with-input),
`t.drizzleFieldWithInput` combines `t.drizzleField` with `t.fieldWithInput`. The `input` fields
become an input object argument, and the resolver still receives the `query` function as its first
argument. This alternative adds an `authorWithInput` lookup to the same public User type.
Install and register WithInputPlugin as described in [Setup](./setup#integration-with-other-plugins):

```ts
builder.queryFields((t) => ({
  authorWithInput: t.drizzleFieldWithInput({
    type: 'users',
    nullable: true,
    input: {
      id: t.input.int({ required: true }),
    },
    resolve: (query, root, args, ctx) => {
      return db.query.users.findFirst(
        query({
          where: { id: args.input.id },
        }),
      );
    },
  }),
}));
```

## Building a query from resolve info [#building-a-query-from-resolve-info]

Use `t.drizzleQueryFromInfo` inside a regular field resolver to combine its GraphQL selection
with Drizzle query options. Pass a table name or Drizzle object/interface ref, along with the
resolver's `context` and `info`. Pass the result directly to Drizzle:

```ts
builder.queryFields((t) => ({
  user: t.field({
    type: User,
    nullable: true,
    args: { id: t.arg.int({ required: true }) },
    resolve: (_root, args, context, info) =>
      db.query.users.findFirst(
        t.drizzleQueryFromInfo('users', {
          context,
          info,
          columns: { id: true },
          where: { id: args.id },
        }),
      ),
  }),
}));
```

Pass `path: ['user']` when the resolver returns a payload containing a `user` field. `paths`
accepts multiple paths. Use a Drizzle ref instead of a table name to select a specific variant
of that table's GraphQL type.

The field builder checks the context and query options against its schema and table. Explicit
columns and relations retain their types; omitted columns are not statically guaranteed, even
if the GraphQL selection loads them. Put filters, selections, ordering, and limits inside the
helper call so they are merged with the planned selection.

With `AsyncSelections: true`, await the result before passing it to Drizzle:

```ts
resolve: async (_root, args, context, info) =>
  db.query.users.findFirst(
    await t.drizzleQueryFromInfo('users', {
      context,
      info,
      where: { id: args.id },
    }),
  ),
```

Without `AsyncSelections`, the helper is typed as synchronous, consistent with the schema's
selection callbacks. There is no per-call async option.


# Ordering and cursors
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/ordering-and-cursors
How a connection orders rows, and the cursors that ordering produces


Connections page with a cursor that records where in the ordering the previous page ended. This
applies to `t.relatedConnection`, `t.drizzleConnection`, and `drizzleConnectionHelpers`.

## Tied timestamps in a feed [#tied-timestamps-in-a-feed]

The [post connection](./connections#page-through-published-posts) orders by `createdAt`, which
can be identical for several posts. Pothos adds a primary-key tie breaker so each post has a
distinct position in the connection.

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ posts(first: 2) { nodes { title } pageInfo { endCursor hasNextPage } } }"
posts: t.drizzleConnection({
  type: 'posts',
  totalCount: () => {
    return db.$count(posts, eq(posts.published, true));
  },
  resolve: (query) => {
    return db.query.posts.findMany(
      query({
        where: { published: true },
        // Three posts share this timestamp. Pothos adds the primary key
        // to the cursor ordering, so traversing pages still visits each once.
        orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' },
      }),
    );
  },
}),
```

### Unique orderings [#unique-orderings]

`orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }` does not describe a unique ordering. Rows with the same timestamp
can be returned in a different order on each query, so paging through the connection may return a row
twice, or skip it.

Pothos adds the primary key to the ordering when the columns you provide are not already unique, so
this:

```ts
orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }
```

is queried as `createdAt desc, id desc`. You can add the tie breaker yourself if you want it in a
different position or direction:

```ts
orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc', id: 'asc' }
```

Orderings that already contain the primary key, or a unique column or constraint whose columns are
all marked `notNull()`, are used as provided. Nullable unique columns are not treated as unique,
because rows containing a `null` are still tied with each other. Uniqueness declared with
`uniqueIndex()` is not detected, so those orderings still get the primary key appended.

Pothos also recognizes composite primary keys declared with `primaryKey({ columns: [...] })`.
Primary-key columns are treated as non-null for ordering; ensure your database enforces that
constraint.

Nothing is appended when Pothos cannot find a key it can rely on, which means tables with no primary
key, and tables whose only unique column is nullable. Those connections keep the ordering you wrote,
so give them a tie breaker yourself.

### Nullable ordering columns [#nullable-ordering-columns]

If you order a connection by a nullable column, paging with a cursor loses rows. `null` is not
greater or less than anything in SQL, so a cursor from a row with a value never returns the rows
where the column is `null`. A cursor from a `null` row only returns the remaining `null` rows, or
nothing when the ordering has no tie breaker. Which rows you lose depends on whether your database
sorts nulls first or last, and on which direction you page. A page requested without a cursor is
complete.

The same applies to an ordering expression that can evaluate to `null`. A nullable column later in
the ordering loses rows the same way, but only among rows that have the same values in the columns
before it.

Order by columns that are `notNull()`, or give the expression a real value to fall back to with
`coalesce`.

### Cursor values and precision [#cursor-values-and-precision]

A cursor stores the values your driver returned to JavaScript, and those values are compared against
the column when the next page is requested. If the value in the cursor is not the value the database
has, the comparison will not match the rows you expect.

This comes up with timestamps. `timestamp({ mode: 'date' })` returns a JavaScript `Date`, which only
holds milliseconds, while a Postgres `timestamptz` column stores microseconds. A row stored at
`.086068` produces a cursor containing `.086`, and `created_at < '.086'` does not match the other
rows in that millisecond, so they are never returned on any page.

There are two ways to avoid this.

The first is to map the column so the full value reaches JavaScript. `mode: 'string'` returns the
timestamp as text, with the microseconds intact:

```ts
export const posts = pgTable('posts', {
  id: serial('id').primaryKey(),
  createdAt: timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true, mode: 'string' }).notNull(),
});
```

The cursor stores that text, and Postgres parses it back to the value it stored. The column is still
what gets ordered and compared, so an index on it is still used. The field is typed as a `string`
rather than a `Date`.

The second is to order by an expression that returns the full value, which lets you keep the `Date`
mapping:

```ts
builder.queryFields((t) => ({
  posts: t.drizzleConnection({
    type: 'posts',
    resolve: (query) => {
      return db.query.posts.findMany(
        query({
          extras: {
            createdAtExact: (table) =>
              sql`to_char(${table.createdAt} AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', 'YYYY-MM-DD"T"HH24:MI:SS.US"Z"')`,
          },
          orderBy: { createdAtExact: 'desc' },
        }),
      );
    },
  }),
}));
```

### Ordering by an expression [#ordering-by-an-expression]

`orderBy` accepts the name of any extra declared in the same query. Pothos orders by the expression,
builds the cursor from the value it returns, and compares the expression when paging:

```ts
query({
  extras: { titleLength: (table) => sql`length(${table.title})` },
  orderBy: { titleLength: 'asc' },
})
```

Extras used this way should be written as a callback. Drizzle aliases the table it queries and passes
that alias to the callback, so an expression built from the imported table object will reference a
name the query does not have.

With `drizzleConnectionHelpers`, declare the extra in `query` rather than in `select`. Only `query`
is read when the ordering is resolved.

The expression also needs to sort in the same order its values compare. A timestamp formatted as
fixed width UTC text sorts the same way it does chronologically, but a local time or variable width
format does not, and will skip rows.


# Query planning
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/query-planning
How the plugin turns a GraphQL query into drizzle queries


This page describes how the plugin turns a GraphQL query into drizzle queries, which is worth
knowing when a schema issues more queries than you expect.

## How fields get their data [#how-fields-get-their-data]

A field either reads its data from a row that has already been loaded, or runs a query of its own.

A field's `select` is planned into the query of the nearest ancestor that runs one: a
`t.drizzleField`, a `t.relation`, a connection, or a [fallback query](./relations#fallback-queries). The field
then reads what it needs off the loaded row, without a query of its own. A field runs its own query
when its `resolve` queries drizzle directly, and when the plugin issues a fallback query for a
relation that is missing from the row.

A field can do both. A `t.drizzleField`, or any other field with a `select`, nested under one of
those ancestors has its `select` planned into the parent's row, and still runs its own query when
it resolves.

A field-level `select` is merged into the same query as its siblings and the type-level selection,
rather than being kept separate for that field. Two selections of the same relation share a place
in that query only when their arguments (`where`, `orderBy`, `limit`, ...) match. When they differ,
the first one planned wins, and the other is loaded with a query of its own. A type-level `select`
is planned before any field's selection, no matter where they appear in the document, and fields
are planned in the order they are selected.

## Compare two orderings of one relation [#compare-two-orderings-of-one-relation]

A client may need both the newest and oldest published posts on one author page:

```graphql
query CompareOrderings {
  author(id: 1) {
    newest: posts {
      title
    }
    oldest: posts(oldestFirst: true) {
      title
    }
  }
}
```

The [published-posts field](./relations#published-posts-and-profiles) translates those arguments
into different database orderings. The two fields cannot reuse the same loaded
relation because their orderings differ. The additional ordering is loaded through a fallback
query.

In this example, selecting one ordering executes one SQL statement; selecting both executes
two. The number of GraphQL field resolvers does not determine the number of database queries.

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ author(id: 1) { newest: posts { title } oldest: posts(oldestFirst: true) { title } } }"
posts: t.relation('posts', {
  args: { oldestFirst: t.arg.boolean() },
  query: (args) => ({
    where: { published: true },
    orderBy: {
      createdAt: args.oldestFirst ? 'asc' : 'desc',
      id: args.oldestFirst ? 'asc' : 'desc',
    },
  }),
}),
```

## Nested selections [#nested-selections]

A `select` function receives `nestedSelection`, which plans the selection beneath the field for the
field's own type. It returns the query config for that table, or a `many` config for a list field.
Any keys you pass in are kept as they were given, so `columns` passed to `nestedSelection` will
still narrow the parent shape:

```ts
const Post = builder.drizzleObject('posts', {
  name: 'Post',
  fields: (t) => ({
    title: t.exposeString('title'),
  }),
});

builder.drizzleObject('users', {
  name: 'User',
  fields: (t) => ({
    previewPosts: t.field({
      type: [Post],
      select: (args, ctx, nestedSelection) => {
        return {
          // what the query selects on the posts, limited to one
          with: {
            posts: nestedSelection({
              where: { published: true },
              orderBy: { id: 'asc' },
              limit: 1,
            }),
          },
        };
      },
      resolve: (user) => user.posts,
    }),
  }),
});
```

`nestedSelection(query, path, type)` takes two more arguments:

* `path`: a list of field names, for selecting a field nested under the field's type. A segment can
  also be written as `{ name, type }` to pin the implementation the field must be found under.
* `type`: a member of an interface or union, to read the selection as that type.

The `nestedSelection` function also carries the `path` and `segments` of the field being planned,
which are described under [Relation queries](./relations#relation-queries).

## Async selections [#async-selections]

When a selection depends on asynchronous request data, enable `AsyncSelections: true` and await
nested plans. [Async selections](./async-selections) covers the builder configuration, supported
callbacks, helper options, and errors caused by unsettled promises.

## Conflicting selections between variants [#conflicting-selections-between-variants]

When a query selects two variants of one table for the same row, either with a fragment on each
under one field, or through a `t.variant` field, the request fails if their `select` options ask
for the same relation with different arguments. The client sees `Unexpected error.`. The
original error is on `error.cause`:

```
PothosValidationError: Type-level selections of Viewer and Admin conflict on relation "posts".
Move the relation arguments to a field-level select on one of the types.
```

The same applies to two variants defining the same `extras` key with different functions
(`... conflict on extra "lowercaseName"`). Both variants describe one row, so their `select`
options are merged into a single query.

To fix this, move the relation with its arguments, or the extra, into the `select` of the field
that needs it on one of the variants. A field-level selection that conflicts with what the row
already holds falls back to a query for that field, rather than failing the request.


# Relations
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/relations
Adding relations to drizzle objects


`t.relation` turns a Drizzle relation into a GraphQL field with its target type and cardinality.
Register the target GraphQL type as well as the relation.

## Published posts and profiles [#published-posts-and-profiles]

The public author page returns published posts. Drafts belong on the [private Viewer](./variants),
so the filter belongs on the relation wherever User can be reached:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle"
posts: t.relation('posts', {
  args: { oldestFirst: t.arg.boolean() },
  query: (args) => ({
    where: { published: true },
    orderBy: {
      createdAt: args.oldestFirst ? 'asc' : 'desc',
      id: args.oldestFirst ? 'asc' : 'desc',
    },
  }),
}),
```

The filter applies whenever this User type is queried. An author with no matching posts returns
an empty list. The `oldestFirst` argument selects the ordering.

To return the Profile object, register its GraphQL type and use `t.relation('profile')`. To
return only its nullable biography, use a [field selection](./selections#only-load-a-profile-when-requested).

## Relation queries [#relation-queries]

`query` accepts a static object or a callback that converts field arguments into Drizzle query
options. Alongside filters and ordering, a relation may use `limit` and `offset`. For example,
this alternative adds offset pagination to the public posts field:

```ts
posts: t.relation('posts', {
  args: { limit: t.arg.int(), offset: t.arg.int() },
  query: (args) => ({
    limit: args.limit ?? 10,
    offset: args.offset ?? 0,
    where: { published: true },
    orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc', id: 'desc' },
  }),
}),
```

The query API enables you to define args and convert them into parameters that will be passed into
the relational query builder. The `query` callback receives `(args, ctx, pathInfo)` where `pathInfo`
describes where in the GraphQL query the relation is being loaded:

* `path`: a list of `ParentType.fieldName` strings, from the root field down to the field being
  resolved (eg. `['Query.user', 'User.posts']`).
* `segments`: one object per entry in `path`, with `field` (the field name), `alias` (the alias used
  in the query, or the field name if none), `parentType` (the name of the type the field is defined
  on), and `isList` (whether the field returns a list).

You can read more about the relation query builder api
[here](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/rqb-v2)

## Fallback queries [#fallback-queries]

A field whose data is not on the row it resolves from is loaded with a fallback query. This happens
when:

* The parent row was not loaded through a `t.drizzleField`, `t.relation`, or connection. This
  covers rows a resolver queried itself, and rows that came from somewhere else entirely.
* A `drizzleField` resolver did not pass the result of `query()` to drizzle.
* A relation's arguments conflict with a sibling selection of the same relation that was planned
  first.

Fallback queries are batched. Every row of a table that needs the same selection in the same tick
is loaded with one `findMany` filtered on the primary key, or on the first unique column for a
table that has no primary key, and the rows are matched back to their parents. If the query does
not return a row for a parent, because it was deleted since it was loaded, or never came from the
table, that field fails with `Unexpected error.`. The original error (`Model users(1) not found`)
is on `error.cause`.

The [alias query](./query-planning#compare-two-orderings-of-one-relation) demonstrates
this fallback: newest and oldest cannot share one loaded posts list.

## Related count [#related-count]

An author’s count must use the same publication filter as the list. Otherwise the number can
reveal that unpublished posts exist:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ author(id: 1) { postCount posts { title } } empty: author(id: 3) { postCount } }"
postCount: t.relatedCount('posts', { where: eq(posts.published, true) }),
```

`t.relatedCount` returns the number of related rows without loading them. Without a `where`,
it counts all rows in the relation.

The `where` option accepts either a static SQL filter or a function that receives the field arguments
and context:

```ts
import { and, eq } from 'drizzle-orm';
import { posts } from './tables';

// In the User fields callback:
publishedPostsCount: t.relatedCount('posts', {
  args: {
    title: t.arg.string(),
  },
  where: (args, ctx) => {
    if (args.title) {
      return and(eq(posts.published, true), eq(posts.title, args.title));
    }

    return eq(posts.published, true);
  },
}),
```

For a many-to-many relation (one defined with `.through(...)`), `t.relatedCount` counts distinct
related rows, so a row reachable through two junction rows counts once. A `t.relatedConnection`'s
`totalCount` counts the rows the connection pages over instead, which is one per junction row,
since that is what the relational query builder returns for the relation.

## Many-to-many relations [#many-to-many-relations]

A post exposes attached Media objects even though the database stores an attachment row. The
`through` relation handles that join; Pothos exposes its target like any other relation:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ author(id: 1) { posts { title media { url uploadedBy { fullName } } mediaConnection(first: 2) { totalCount nodes { url } } } } }"
builder.drizzleObject('posts', {
  name: 'Post',
  select: {},
  fields: (t) => ({
    id: t.exposeID('id'),
    title: t.exposeString('title'),
    author: t.relation('author'),
    media: t.relation('media'),
    mediaConnection: t.relatedConnection('media', {
      query: { orderBy: { id: 'asc' } },
      totalCount: true,
    }),
  }),
});
export const Media = builder.drizzleObject('media', {
  name: 'Media',
  fields: (t) => ({ url: t.exposeString('url'), uploadedBy: t.relation('uploadedBy') }),
});
```

`t.relation` and `t.relatedConnection` expose the Media type directly; no GraphQL type for the
junction table is needed.

## Related field [#related-field]

The `t.relatedField` method allows you to define a field based on a relation that uses custom
selections, including aggregations like counts. This is useful when you want to expose derived data
from a relation without loading the full related records.

For a simple count, prefer `t.relatedCount`. Its equivalent using `t.relatedField` illustrates
how `buildFilter` restricts an expression to the parent's related rows:

```ts
import { and, eq } from 'drizzle-orm';
import { posts } from './tables';

builder.drizzleNode('users', {
  name: 'User',
  id: { column: (user) => user.id },
  fields: (t) => ({
    firstName: t.exposeString('firstName'),
    // Count only this author’s published posts
    postsCount: t.relatedField('posts', {
      type: 'Int',
      // buildFilter creates the correct WHERE clause for the relation
      select: (buildFilter) => {
        return {
          extras: {
            postsCount: (parent) => {
              return db.$count(
                posts,
                and(buildFilter(parent), eq(posts.published, true)),
              );
            },
          },
        };
      },
      resolve: (user) => user.postsCount,
    }),
  }),
});
```

`buildFilter(parent)` includes the relation's join conditions and any filter defined on the
relation. Combine it with the conditions your field needs, then return the selected value from
`resolve`. Use this helper for custom expressions that `t.relatedCount` does not cover.

`t.relatedField` also accepts the normal field options (`description`, `deprecationReason`,
`extensions`, and options added by other plugins like `authScopes`). Its `resolve` may be async,
and receives the resolve `info` as its fourth argument.


# Relay nodes
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/relay
Defining refetchable nodes with the Drizzle plugin




The Relay plugin supplies node IDs and cursor connections. Register it with Drizzle as shown in
[Setup](./setup#integration-with-other-plugins); [Connections](./connections) covers pagination.

<Callout type="warn" title="Authorize direct node lookups">
  Defining a node creates a direct lookup through `node` and `nodes`. These lookups bypass custom
  root resolvers, so permission checks or visibility filters on a list or parent field do not protect
  node refetches. An encoded global ID is an identifier, not proof of permission.

  With Scope Auth, require scopes on the `node` and `nodes` fields, put scopes on the `Node`
  interface or each node type, or disable the lookup fields. You can also enforce visibility where the
  node loads, so inaccessible records look missing. See
  [Relay node authorization](/docs/plugins/scope-auth/relay-nodes) for each option and its
  limits.
</Callout>

## Define a node [#define-a-node]

`builder.drizzleNode` uses the same fields and selections as `builder.drizzleObject`, and adds
an ID and a root node lookup. The example User uses its integer primary key:

```ts
builder.drizzleNode('users', {
  name: 'User',
  id: { column: (user) => user.id },
  fields: (t) => ({ firstName: t.exposeString('firstName') }),
});
```

This minimal alternative shows the node options. The example User adds full name, profile,
and published posts to the same type. Other ID field options can be passed alongside `column`;
for a composite primary key, `column` can return a list of columns.

## Refetch a public author [#refetch-a-public-author]

The ID returned by User can be passed back to
`node` to fetch the author with a new selection:

```graphql
query RefetchAuthor {
  node(id: "VXNlcjox") {
    ... on User {
      fullName
      posts {
        title
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The [refetch operation](/playground?example=plugin-drizzle\&op=7) uses the ID of User 1. The node
returns the same public fields as the author lookup, including only published posts.

## Authorize the node load path [#authorize-the-node-load-path]

The public User type here can be refetched by anyone. Its
[published-posts relation](./relations#published-posts-and-profiles) applies the publication filter
wherever User is reached, including through `node`. Post stays an ordinary Drizzle object;
defining a public feed does not also make individual drafts globally refetchable.


# Selections
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/selections
Selecting the columns and relations your fields need


Selections describe the database data a GraphQL field needs. The example User starts with
`select: {}` so requesting one field does not load unrelated columns or a profile.

## Field selections [#field-selections]

An exposed column, such as `t.exposeString('firstName')`, contributes its own selection. A custom
resolver must declare the columns it reads:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ author(id: 1) { fullName } }"
fullName: t.string({
  select: { columns: { firstName: true, lastName: true } },
  resolve: (user) => `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`,
}),
```

## Only load a profile when requested [#only-load-a-profile-when-requested]

A biography is a string in GraphQL, but it comes from the optional profile relation. The field
selects that relation only when requested:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ author(id: 1) { fullName bio } missingProfile: author(id: 3) { fullName bio } }"
bio: t.string({
  nullable: true,
  select: { with: { profile: true } },
  resolve: (user) => user.profile?.bio,
}),
```

A missing profile returns null. A name-only query does not load the profile; adding `bio` adds
the relation to the database query.

## Computed SQL values [#computed-sql-values]

The same mechanism supports SQL expressions through `extras`. For example, a field can select
`lowercaseName` only when the GraphQL operation requests it:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ author(id: 1) { fullName lowercaseName } }"
lowercaseName: t.string({
  select: {
    extras: {
      lowercaseName: (users, { sql }) => sql<string>`lower(${users.firstName})`,
    },
  },
  resolve: (user) => user.lowercaseName,
}),
```

## Type selections [#type-selections]

By default, a `drizzleObject` gives its resolvers access to all columns of the table. A type-level
`select` replaces that default and makes its selected data available to every field resolver.
This alternative always loads the name, profile, and expression:

```ts
const User = builder.drizzleObject('users', {
  name: 'User',
  select: {
    columns: {
      firstName: true,
      lastName: true,
    },
    with: {
      profile: true,
    },
    extras: {
      lowercaseName: (users, { sql }) => sql<string>`lower(${users.firstName})`
    },
  },
  fields: (t) => {
    return {
      fullName: t.string({
        resolve: (user, args, ctx, info) => `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`,
      }),
      bio: t.string({
        nullable: true,
        resolve: (user) => user.profile?.bio,
      }),
      lowercaseName: t.string({
        resolve: (user) => user.lowercaseName,
      }),
    };
  },
});
```

Any selections added to the type will be available to consume in all resolvers. Columns that are not
selected can still be exposed as before.

Use type selections for data required whenever the type is loaded, and field selections for data
needed by a particular field. Both are merged into the parent query; they do not make each field
an independent database query. See [Query planning](./query-planning).

With `ScopeAuthPlugin`, scope checks that read the parent see what its type loads (its `select`, or
every column), even for a row returned from a plain `t.field`. A row missing that data is reloaded,
so a row that no longer exists fails the field with `Unexpected error.`. To return a deleted row,
load it with a `t.drizzleField` query before deleting it. Only top-level keys are checked, so a row
with a partly loaded relation isn't reloaded.


# Setup
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/setup
Setting up the Drizzle plugin


Pass your existing Drizzle client and relations to the plugin. These guides assume familiarity
with Drizzle; use its [driver setup](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/connect-overview) and
[relations documentation](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/relations-v2) to configure the database.

## Installing [#installing]

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="npm">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="npm">
      npm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="pnpm">
      pnpm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="yarn">
      yarn
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="bun">
      bun
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>

  <CodeBlockTab value="npm">
    ```bash
    npm install --save @pothos/plugin-drizzle
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="pnpm">
    ```bash
    pnpm add @pothos/plugin-drizzle
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="yarn">
    ```bash
    yarn add @pothos/plugin-drizzle
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="bun">
    ```bash
    bun add @pothos/plugin-drizzle
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

The plugin requires Drizzle's relational query builder v2. See the
[version requirements](/docs/plugins/drizzle) before installing or upgrading Drizzle.

## Configure the builder [#configure-the-builder]

```ts
// builder.ts
import SchemaBuilder from '@pothos/core';
import DrizzlePlugin from '@pothos/plugin-drizzle';
import { getTableConfig } from 'drizzle-orm/sqlite-core';
import { db } from './database';
import { relations } from './tables';

export interface PothosTypes {
  DrizzleRelations: typeof relations;
  Context: { userId: number };
}

export const builder = new SchemaBuilder<PothosTypes>({
  plugins: [DrizzlePlugin],
  drizzle: { client: db, getTableConfig, relations },
});
```

`DrizzleRelations` provides the table and relation types used by Pothos. Import `getTableConfig`
from the dialect used by your client (`sqlite-core` above, or `pg-core` / `mysql-core`). `client`
may also be a function `(ctx) => db` for a request-specific client. The examples use
[request context](/docs/guide/context) to supply the current `userId`.

Use this builder to [define GraphQL types and fields](./objects), then call `builder.toSchema()`.

## Integration with other plugins [#integration-with-other-plugins]

Install and register `@pothos/plugin-relay` to use `drizzleNode` and connection fields:

```ts
import RelayPlugin from '@pothos/plugin-relay';

// In the builder options:
plugins: [RelayPlugin, DrizzlePlugin],
relay: { nodesOnConnection: true },
```

`nodesOnConnection` adds the `nodes` convenience field used in these guides. Without it,
select `edges { node { ... } }` instead.

The [with-input plugin](../with-input) is another optional integration. To use
`t.drizzleFieldWithInput`, install `@pothos/plugin-with-input`, import it, and add it to the
builder's plugins:

```ts
import WithInputPlugin from '@pothos/plugin-with-input';

// In the builder options:
plugins: [RelayPlugin, WithInputPlugin, DrizzlePlugin],
```

## Plugin options [#plugin-options]

* `client`: the drizzle client, or a function returning one from the request context.
* `getTableConfig`: the `getTableConfig` of your dialect, used to read primary keys and unique
  constraints.
* `relations`: the relations passed to `drizzle()`.
* `defaultConnectionSize` / `maxConnectionSize`: the page size a connection uses when the query
  does not ask for one (defaults to 20), and the largest size it will accept (defaults to 100).
  Both can also be set per field with `defaultSize` and `maxSize`.
* `filterConnectionTotalCount`: see [Connection totalCount](./connections#connection-totalcount).
* `skipDeferredFragments`: selections inside a `@defer` fragment are left out of the planned query
  by default, and the fragment's fields are loaded through [fallback queries](./relations#fallback-queries)
  when it resolves. Set this to `false` to plan deferred selections with the rest of the query.

`skipDeferredFragments` controls query planning; it does not enable incremental execution. The application
must register the defer directive and use an executor, server transport, and client that support
the same incremental delivery protocol. With GraphQL.js 17, ordinary `execute` rejects schemas
containing `@defer` or `@stream`; incremental execution uses `experimentalExecuteIncrementally`.
For a server integration, see [GraphQL Yoga's defer and stream setup](https://the-guild.dev/graphql/yoga-server/docs/features/defer-stream),
which uses `@graphql-yoga/plugin-defer-stream`. Check the integration's supported versions when
choosing an executor and client; adding directives or changing `skipDeferredFragments` alone is
not sufficient.


# Type variants
URL: /docs/plugins/drizzle/variants
How to define multiple GraphQL types based on the same drizzle table


A variant gives another GraphQL representation to the same database row. The publishing API
uses public User fields for author pages and a private Viewer for the signed-in account.

The API has three parts:

* `variant` registers an additional type instead of naming the primary type with `name`.
* `t.variant` returns another representation of the same row.
* A relation's `type` option can select a variant using its returned object ref.

## A single object variant [#a-single-object-variant]

Use `variant` to define Viewer alongside the primary User type. `t.variant('users')` exposes
the public representation of the same row:

```ts
const Viewer = builder.drizzleObject('users', {
  variant: 'Viewer',
  select: {},
  fields: (t) => {
    return {
      id: t.exposeID('id'),
      user: t.variant('users'),
      drafts: t.relation('posts', {
        query: {
        where: { published: false },
        orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc', id: 'desc' },
      },
      }),
    };
  },
});
```

## A viewer with role-specific fields [#a-viewer-with-role-specific-fields]

When viewer fields differ by role, Viewer can instead be an interface with object variants
for each role. The following definition uses this structure; [Interfaces](./interfaces) explains
its implementations:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ me { __typename email user { fullName } drafts { title } } }"
export const Viewer = builder.drizzleInterface('users', {
  variant: 'Viewer',
  select: { columns: { id: true, role: true } },
  resolveType: (user) => (user.role === 'editor' ? 'EditorViewer' : 'AuthorViewer'),
  fields: (t) => ({
    user: t.variant('users'),
    email: t.exposeString('email'),
    drafts: t.relation('posts', {
      query: { where: { published: false }, orderBy: { id: 'asc' } },
    }),
  }),
});
```

The root lookup uses the authenticated context ID. It does not accept an arbitrary author's ID:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ me { __typename email drafts { title } } }"
me: t.drizzleField({
  type: Viewer,
  nullable: true,
  resolve: (query, _root, _args, ctx) => {
    return db.query.users.findFirst(
      query({
        where: { id: ctx.userId },
      }),
    );
  },
}),
```

Maya (`userId: 1`) sees “Planning the spring exchange”; Leo (`userId: 2`) sees “Saving rainwater.”
The interface and variants describe the shapes; the root lookup restricts ownership. Public
author fields and post connections return published posts only.

## Conditionally expose another variant [#conditionally-expose-another-variant]

The publishing User also exposes its Viewer conditionally. Define that field after Viewer is registered,
which avoids a circular reference between their definitions:

```typescript playground example="plugin-drizzle" query="{ own: author(id: 1) { viewer { email drafts { title } } } other: author(id: 2) { viewer { email } } }"
builder.drizzleObjectField('users', 'viewer', (t) =>
  t.variant(Viewer, {
    select: { columns: { id: true } },
    isNull: (user, _args, ctx) => user.id !== ctx.userId,
  }),
);
```

The ownership check is essential: without it an arbitrary author's public row could reveal that
author's drafts. `isNull` makes the variant field null when its parent is another account.

A variant field accepts a `select` just like other fields. Here it loads `id` for the ownership
check; the target variant contributes the selections required by its own fields.

## Relation variants [#relation-variants]

To use a different representation of a related row, pass its object ref to `t.relation`'s `type`
option. The variant must represent the relation's target table. For example, this alternative
adds a compact PostSummary representation and selects it for a public author's posts:

```ts
const PostSummary = builder.drizzleObject('posts', {
  variant: 'PostSummary',
  fields: (t) => ({ title: t.exposeString('title') }),
});

builder.drizzleObjectField('users', 'postSummaries', (t) =>
  t.relation('posts', {
    type: PostSummary,
    query: {
      where: { published: true },
      orderBy: { id: 'asc' },
    },
  }),
);
```

Two variants selected for the same row have their type-level selections merged. Conflicting
relation arguments or extras can fail; see
[Conflicting selections between variants](./query-planning#conflicting-selections-between-variants).


# Connections
URL: /docs/plugins/prisma-next/connections
Relay connections backed by Prisma Collections


Connections add cursor pagination to a list. They require the [Relay plugin](../relay). Use
`t.prismaConnection` to paginate a model's rows, and `t.relatedConnection` to paginate a relation.

## Paginate a query field [#paginate-a-query-field]

```ts
builder.queryFields((t) => ({
  posts: t.prismaConnection({
    type: 'Post',
    query: { where: { published: 1 }, orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' } },
    totalCount: true,
  }),
}));
```

Clients request pages with `first` and `after`, or `last` and `before`. For example:

```graphql
{
  posts(first: 10) {
    edges { node { title } }
    pageInfo { endCursor hasNextPage }
    totalCount
  }
}
```

## Paginate a relation [#paginate-a-relation]

To paginate a relation, such as a user's posts, use `t.relatedConnection`:

```typescript playground example="plugin-prisma-next" query="{ author(id: 1) { fullName postConnection(first: 1) { totalCount edges { node { title } } pageInfo { endCursor hasNextPage } } } }"
// Pages through the relation inside the query that loads the user.
builder.prismaObjectField('User', 'postConnection', (t) =>
  t.relatedConnection('posts', {
    query: { where: { published: 1 } },
    totalCount: true,
  }),
);
```

It takes the same options as `t.prismaConnection` except `collection`. `totalCount` counts the rows
matching `query.where`, unless [`filterConnectionTotalCount`](./setup#plugin-options) is `false`.

## Configure a connection [#configure-a-connection]

`t.prismaConnection` takes:

* `query`: `{ where, orderBy }`, or `(args, ctx) => ({ where, orderBy })`. Rows are ordered by the
  primary key when `orderBy` is omitted. See [Ordering and cursors](#ordering-and-cursors).
* `defaultSize` / `maxSize`: page sizes, or `(args, ctx) => number`. Default to the plugin's
  [connection size options](./setup#plugin-options).
* `totalCount`: `true` counts the rows matching `query.where`. Pass
  `(parent, args, ctx, info) => number` to count them yourself. The count only runs when
  `totalCount` is selected.
* `args`: extra arguments for filtering or sorting. The Relay pagination arguments are added automatically.
* `collection`: an optional starting ORM query, returned by `(parent, args, ctx, info) => Collection`.
  See [Use a custom Collection](#use-a-custom-collection).

Don't call `orderBy()`, `include()`, `limit()`, `offset()`, `cursor()`, `distinct()` or
`distinctOn()` on the Collection you return. The first two are type errors, and the rest throw
before any SQL runs.

Connection and edge types can be customized as with the [Relay plugin](../relay), including
`edgesNullable` and `nodeNullable`.

## Ordering and cursors [#ordering-and-cursors]

A connection's `query.orderBy` takes columns of the model, each with a direction, as a
[relation's](./relations#filtering-and-sorting) does. You can't order a connection by relation
columns, aggregates or expressions. Nullable columns sort nulls last unless you set `nulls`:

```ts
query: { orderBy: { score: { direction: 'desc', nulls: 'first' } } },
```

If the order doesn't include a unique key, the plugin adds the primary key to the end, in the same
direction as the last column. If the primary key can't be ordered, it uses the first non-null unique
key that can.

To let clients choose the order, pass a function of the arguments:

```typescript playground example="plugin-prisma-next" query="{ posts(first: 2, newestFirst: true) { totalCount edges { node { title } } pageInfo { endCursor hasNextPage } } }"
posts: t.prismaConnection({
  type: 'Post',
  totalCount: true,
  args: { newestFirst: t.arg.boolean() },
  // Chooses the direction per request; the plugin reverses it for backward pages.
  query: (args) => ({
    where: { published: 1 },
    orderBy: { id: args.newestFirst ? 'desc' : 'asc' },
  }),
}),
```

Cursors contain the values of the ordered columns and clients can read them, so don't order by
columns clients shouldn't see.

A timestamp read as a JavaScript `Date` only keeps milliseconds, so you can't order by one with a
precision above 3. A plain `DateTime` is fine. On PostgreSQL, use `TimestamptzTemporal` for more
precise timestamps.

An invalid `orderBy` in a `query` object throws when the schema is built. If a `query` function
returns one, that request fails.

## Use a custom Collection [#use-a-custom-collection]

Use `collection` for an existing ORM query or to run code before the connection loads. For example,
check access before returning the query for draft posts:

```ts
builder.queryField('drafts', (t) =>
  t.prismaConnection({
    type: 'Post',
    collection: (_root, _args, ctx) => {
      if (!ctx.isAdmin) {
        throw new Error('Not allowed.');
      }
      return db.orm.Post.where({ published: 0 });
    },
    query: { orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' } },
  }),
);
```

The callback can be async. [Queries and selections](./queries) explains its arguments and how
`collection` and `query` combine.

## Custom connections [#custom-connections]

Use `prismaConnectionHelpers` with `t.connection` when a connection's nodes are a different model
than the rows being paged, or when your resolver needs to work with the loaded rows. For
everything else, use `t.prismaConnection` and `t.relatedConnection`.

For example, a post's `commenters` connection pages through comments but returns each comment's
author. The helper takes a model name or a Prisma type ref, plus `query`, `defaultSize`, `maxSize`,
`totalCount` and `args`. `totalCount` takes `true`, but not a function.

`select` sets what is loaded for each comment. Use `nodeSelection()` for the relation that holds
the node. A helper can only have one. Other relations can be selected with `true`.
`resolveNode` returns the node for each comment:

```ts
import { prismaConnectionHelpers } from '@pothos/plugin-prisma-next';

const commenters = prismaConnectionHelpers(builder, 'Comment', {
  query: { orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' } },
  totalCount: true,
  select: (nodeSelection) => ({ createdAt: true, author: nodeSelection() }),
  resolveNode: (comment) => comment.author,
});

builder.prismaObjectField('Post', 'commenters', (t) =>
  t.connection(
    {
      type: User,
      select: (args, ctx) => ({
        comments: commenters.getQuery(args, ctx),
      }),
      resolve: (post, args, ctx) => commenters.resolve(post.comments, args, ctx),
    },
    {
      fields: (connection) => ({
        totalCount: connection.int({ resolve: (page) => page.totalCount }),
      }),
    },
  ),
);
```

`getQuery` loads one page of comments with the post, and the count when the connection selects a
field named `totalCount`. `resolve` builds the connection from the rows that `getQuery` or `load`
loaded. You can also pass it rows you loaded yourself with the same order and paging. `totalCount`
is only set for a list that `getQuery` or `load` loaded, or when you pass a count. Without
`resolveNode`, the rows are the nodes, and the connection's `type` should be the helper's `ref`.

Call `getQuery` at the top level of the connection field's own `select`, not inside another
relation's entry. To put the connection on another type, make that type a [variant](./variants) of
the model the field is on.

`select` and `query` also receive the field's arguments and context. Add the helper's `args` to the
field with `args: commenters.getArgs()`.

To count the rows yourself, for example on MySQL where Prisma can't count them yet, pass the count
to `resolve`: `commenters.resolve(rows, args, ctx, { totalCount })`.

### Load a page in your resolver [#load-a-page-in-your-resolver]

On a root field, use `load` to page a Collection of the helper's model. It loads the page, along
with whatever the query selects on the nodes, in one statement, and the count when `totalCount` is
selected. The Collection has the same restrictions as a `t.prismaConnection`'s `collection`. Pass
the rows to `resolve`. With `resolveNode`, each edge also has its row, so edge fields can read it:

```ts
builder.queryField('postCommenters', (t) =>
  t.connection(
    {
      type: User,
      args: { ...commenters.getArgs(), postId: t.arg.id({ required: true }) },
      resolve: async (_root, args, ctx, info) => {
        const comments = db.orm.Comment.where({ postId: String(args.postId) });
        const rows = await commenters.load(comments, args, ctx, info);
        return commenters.resolve(rows, args, ctx);
      },
    },
    {
      fields: (connection) => ({
        totalCount: connection.int({ resolve: (page) => page.totalCount }),
      }),
    },
    {
      fields: (edge) => ({
        commentedAt: edge.string({ resolve: (comment) => comment.createdAt.toISOString() }),
      }),
    },
  ),
);
```

`load` returns one extra row, which `resolve` uses to tell whether there is another page. Pass the
list to `resolve` unchanged.


# Prisma ORM 8 plugin
URL: /docs/plugins/prisma-next
An experimental Pothos plugin for the Prisma ORM 8 collection client




This plugin integrates [Prisma ORM 8](https://github.com/prisma/orm) with Pothos to build
a strongly typed GraphQL API from your Prisma models. Expose database fields and relations, add
computed fields, and support Relay nodes and paginated connections. Your GraphQL types and fields can
have different names and shapes from the underlying models.

Each field declares the columns and relations it needs, and the plugin loads what the incoming
GraphQL query uses. Relations, counts and connection pages load with their parent, usually in one
SQL statement per root field, so you don't need a resolver or database call for every relation.
Field types are inferred from your Prisma contract.

<Callout type="warn" title="Experimental">
  This plugin targets Prisma ORM `8.0.0-rc.23` exactly. Its API, and Prisma's, may change in any
  release. For Prisma ORM 7, use [the Prisma plugin](/docs/plugins/prisma).
</Callout>

The [playground example](/playground?example=plugin-prisma-next) runs the examples below against
SQLite in the browser, and its **SQL** tab shows the statements each query runs.

## Example [#example]

With a [configured builder](/docs/plugins/prisma-next/setup), define the posts your API exposes
and their author relation. These examples use the playground's `Post` and `User` models:

```typescript playground example="plugin-prisma-next"
builder.prismaObject('Post', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    id: t.exposeID('id'),
    title: t.exposeString('title'),
    author: t.relation('author'),
  }),
});
```

`fullName` is a computed field. Its `select` lists the columns the resolver reads:

```typescript playground example="plugin-prisma-next"
builder.prismaObject('User', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    id: t.exposeID('id'),
    email: t.exposeString('email'),
    // Selects its columns only when a query asks for this field.
    fullName: t.string({
      select: ['firstName', 'lastName'],
      resolve: (user) => `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`,
    }),
  }),
});
```

Add a recent-posts query that returns the ten latest published posts:

```typescript playground example="plugin-prisma-next" query="{ recentPosts { title author { fullName } } }"
builder.queryType({
  fields: (t) => ({
    recentPosts: t.prismaField({
      type: ['Post'],
      query: { where: { published: 1 }, orderBy: { id: 'desc' }, limit: 10 },
    }),
  }),
});
```

For `{ recentPosts { title author { fullName } } }`, the posts and their authors load in one SQL
statement, including the columns needed to compute each author's name.

## Relay connections [#relay-connections]

With the [Relay plugin](/docs/plugins/relay), `t.relatedConnection` adds a paginated list of
published posts to an author profile:

```typescript playground example="plugin-prisma-next" query="{ author(id: 1) { fullName postConnection(first: 1) { totalCount edges { node { title } } pageInfo { endCursor hasNextPage } } } }"
// Pages through the relation inside the query that loads the user.
builder.prismaObjectField('User', 'postConnection', (t) =>
  t.relatedConnection('posts', {
    query: { where: { published: 1 } },
    totalCount: true,
  }),
);
```

`t.prismaConnection` does the same for query fields. See
[Connections](/docs/plugins/prisma-next/connections).

## Next steps [#next-steps]

To get started, follow [Setup](/docs/plugins/prisma-next/setup), then read
[Queries and selections](/docs/plugins/prisma-next/queries), [Objects](/docs/plugins/prisma-next/objects) and [Relations](/docs/plugins/prisma-next/relations).
For an existing Prisma ORM 7 schema, see [Migrating from the Prisma plugin](/docs/plugins/prisma-next/migrating-from-prisma).


# Indirect relations
URL: /docs/plugins/prisma-next/indirect-relations
Loading relations for fields that aren't t.relation


Use [`t.relation`](./relations) for a direct relation, including a renamed or filtered field.
Use `t.field` with a `select` when the field goes through a join model, wraps the rows in another
GraphQL type, or needs its own resolver logic.

A field's `select` function gets `nestedSelection` as its third argument. Use it as the value for
a relation, and the plugin loads that relation in the parent's query, with whatever the client
selects on the field's type:

```ts
const Post = builder.prismaObject('Post', {
  fields: (t) => ({ title: t.exposeString('title') }),
});

builder.prismaObject('User', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    publishedPosts: t.field({
      type: [Post],
      select: (args, ctx, nestedSelection) => ({
        posts: nestedSelection({ where: { published: 1 } }),
      }),
      resolve: (user) => user.posts,
    }),
  }),
});
```

For this filtered field alone, prefer
`publishedPosts: t.relation('posts', { query: { where: { published: 1 } } })`.

With `{ posts: true }` instead, the plugin only loads each post's columns. Anything selected
under the field, such as a post's `author`, needs an extra batched query. Use `nestedSelection`
whenever the field's type has relations or selects of its own.

`nestedSelection` takes an optional object with the same options as a
[relation entry](./objects#selections), plus `path`:

* `where`, `orderBy`, `limit`, `offset`: the relation's
  [query options](./relations#filtering-and-sorting). A to-one relation takes none.
* `select`: anything else to load for each row, on top of what the query selects.
* `path`: the path to a nested field to read the selection from. A segment can be written as
  `{ name, type }` to only read the field inside a fragment on that type.
* `type`: the type to read the selection as, when the field returns an interface or union. You can
  pass anything a field's `type` takes, or a model's name for its default type. The type's model
  must be the relation's target, and the query and rows are typed for that model.

The rows only include the primary key and the selected columns, not every column.

## Selecting fields from a nested GraphQL field [#selecting-fields-from-a-nested-graphql-field]

When the field returns a plain object type that wraps the rows, pass the `path` to the field
inside it that returns the relation's type:

```ts
const PostPreview = builder.objectRef<typeof Post.$inferType>('PostPreview').implement({
  fields: (t) => ({
    post: t.field({ type: Post, resolve: (post) => post }),
  }),
});

builder.prismaObject('User', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    postPreviews: t.field({
      type: [PostPreview],
      select: (args, ctx, nestedSelection) => ({
        // Load the selection under `postPreviews.post` for the 2 newest posts
        posts: nestedSelection({ orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }, limit: 2, path: ['post'] }),
      }),
      resolve: (user) => user.posts,
    }),
  }),
});
```

## Selecting as a specific type [#selecting-as-a-specific-type]

When the field returns an interface or union, use `type` to pick the object type to read the
selection as. Fragments on other types are ignored:

```ts
const Comment = builder.prismaObject('Comment', {
  // Loaded whenever a Comment is queried, so resolveType can read it
  select: ['postId'],
  fields: (t) => ({ body: t.exposeString('body') }),
});

const Activity = builder.unionType('Activity', {
  types: [Post, Comment],
  resolveType: (row) => ('postId' in row ? 'Comment' : 'Post'),
});

builder.prismaObject('User', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    recentActivity: t.field({
      type: [Activity],
      select: (args, ctx, nestedSelection) => ({
        posts: nestedSelection({ limit: 5, type: Post }),
        comments: nestedSelection({ limit: 5, type: Comment }),
      }),
      resolve: (user) => [...user.posts, ...user.comments],
    }),
  }),
});
```

## Join models [#join-models]

Relations defined with `rel.manyToMany` work with `t.relation` and `nestedSelection` like any
other to-many relation.

When the join table is its own model, give the relation to the join model a `select`, and use
`nestedSelection` inside it. Here comments join users to the posts they commented on:

```ts
builder.prismaObject('User', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    commentedPosts: t.field({
      type: [Post],
      select: (args, ctx, nestedSelection) => ({
        comments: { orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }, select: { post: nestedSelection() } },
      }),
      resolve: (user) => user.comments.map((comment) => comment.post),
    }),
  }),
});
```

Everything still loads in the parent's query. To load only one variant of a relation's model, add
`type` to the relation's entry, with the variant's ref or model name:
`{ type: Bug, select: { reviewer: true } }`.


# Model inheritance
URL: /docs/plugins/prisma-next/inheritance
Exposing inherited Prisma models through a GraphQL interface


When your Prisma contract defines inherited models, such as a `Task` that can be a `Bug` or a
`Feature`, expose their shared fields through a GraphQL interface. Each kind gets an object type,
and the plugin chooses the right type for each row automatically.

For multiple GraphQL views of a single Prisma model, use [Type variants](./variants).

## Define the interface and its objects [#define-the-interface-and-its-objects]

This example assumes a contract with `Task`, its `Bug` and `Feature` variants, and a `User` model
with a `tasks` relation. `Bug` also has an optional `reviewer` relation to `User`. Use the builder
and imported `db` from [Setup](./setup), with `User` already defined as a GraphQL type.

```ts
const Task = builder.prismaInterface('Task', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    id: t.exposeID('id'),
    title: t.exposeString('title'),
    owner: t.relation('owner'),
  }),
});

const Bug = builder.prismaObject('Bug', {
  interfaces: [Task],
  select: { reviewer: true },
  fields: (t) => ({
    severity: t.exposeString('severity'),
    reviewerEmail: t.string({
      nullable: true,
      resolve: (bug) => bug.reviewer?.email,
    }),
  }),
});

builder.prismaObject('Feature', {
  interfaces: [Task],
  fields: (t) => ({ priority: t.exposeInt('priority') }),
});

builder.queryFields((t) => ({
  tasks: t.prismaField({ type: [Task] }),
  bugs: t.prismaField({ type: [Bug] }),
}));
```

Define an object for each variant in the contract. You don't need a `resolveType`. Clients can
query shared fields and add fragments for variant-specific fields:

```graphql
{
  tasks {
    id
    title
    ... on Bug {
      severity
      reviewerEmail
    }
    ... on Feature {
      priority
    }
  }
}
```

A variant's `select` works like it does on any other type. Here `Bug` loads its reviewer so
`reviewerEmail` can read it. Anything in the interface's `select` is available to the types that
implement it too.

## Query a variant [#query-a-variant]

Use a variant's type on a field to return only that variant's rows. To filter on the variant's
own fields, pass `where` as a function:

```ts
builder.queryField('highSeverityBugs', (t) =>
  t.prismaField({
    type: [Bug],
    query: { where: (bug) => bug.severity.eq('high') },
  }),
);
```

If you pass your own `collection`, start from the base model narrowed to the variant, such as
`db.orm.Task.variant('bug')`. This is what the plugin uses when you omit `collection`.

## Expose related variants [#expose-related-variants]

For a relation to `Task`, return the interface to include every variant, or pass a variant's ref
as `type` to narrow the field:

```ts
builder.prismaObjectFields('User', (t) => ({
  tasks: t.relation('tasks', { type: Task }),
  bugs: t.relation('tasks', { type: Bug }),
}));
```

The plugin sometimes runs an extra batched query to load what each variant's type needs.

When a variant is stored in its own table, a relation to it can filter and sort by the variant's
own fields, but not by fields inherited from the base model. To use both, start from the base
Collection narrowed with `variant()`, as in the previous section.

Custom resolvers that load rows can use [collectionFromInfo](./relations#returning-rows-from-other-fields)
to load what the query selects. Variant rows loaded this way can also be returned through a
compatible `prismaInterface`. The plugin loads anything else it needs to resolve their type.

## Mutations [#mutations]

When a `t.prismaField` returns `Bug`, its resolver receives a Collection for
`orm.Task.variant('bug')`. `variant('bug')` only narrows to bugs, and `update()` and `delete()` act
on the first match, so add a filter such as `where({ id })` to change one task.

### Return an updated record [#return-an-updated-record]

Some Prisma write methods return only the base model's columns when the variant has its own
table. For example, an updated `Feature` may be missing its `priority`. Use `updateAndCount()`
to make the change, then `first()` on the same filtered Collection to read the response.

When the field returns the `Task` interface, the plugin may run another query after the update
to load a relation such as `Bug.reviewer`.

### Return a deleted record [#return-a-deleted-record]

A deleted row cannot be read again. To return a deleted bug with its reviewer, return the `Bug`
object type, or prepare the query with `collectionFromInfo({ ..., typeName: 'Bug' })` before
calling `delete()`. Either way the reviewer is loaded as part of the delete.
`collectionFromInfo` requires `typeName` for a Collection that uses `variant('bug')`.

For a variant stored in its own table, Prisma's `delete()` result contains only the base model's
columns too. Return an ID or a payload that does not need the missing fields. Avoid `@defer` on a
deleted record, because deferred fields may need to read the row after it is gone.

### Upsert a variant [#upsert-a-variant]

For variants stored in the base model's table, `upsert()` can match a unique key belonging to a
different variant. For example, `Task.variant('bug').upsert(...)` can update a feature with that
key and return it as a bug. Check the existing task's kind before choosing whether to create or
update when your mutation must preserve it.


# Interfaces
URL: /docs/plugins/prisma-next/interfaces
GraphQL interfaces backed by contract models


`builder.prismaInterface` defines a GraphQL interface for a Prisma model. It takes the same
options as `builder.prismaObject`.

Building on [Type variants](./variants), update the `User` and `Viewer` definitions to share a
`Person` interface. Here `resolveType` chooses `Viewer` for the signed-in user's own row, and `User`
for other authors:

```ts
const Person = builder.prismaInterface('User', {
  variant: 'Person',
  resolveType: (user, ctx) => (user.id === ctx.userId ? 'Viewer' : 'User'),
  fields: (t) => ({
    id: t.exposeID('id'),
    firstName: t.exposeString('firstName'),
  }),
});

builder.prismaObject('User', {
  interfaces: [Person],
  fields: (t) => ({
    posts: t.relation('posts', { query: { where: { published: 1 } } }),
  }),
});

builder.prismaObject('User', {
  variant: 'Viewer',
  interfaces: [Person],
  fields: (t) => ({
    email: t.exposeString('email'),
    drafts: t.relation('posts', { query: { where: { published: 0 } } }),
  }),
});

builder.queryField('author', (t) =>
  t.prismaField({
    type: Person,
    nullable: true,
    args: { id: t.arg.id({ required: true }) },
    query: (args) => ({ where: { id: String(args.id) } }),
  }),
);
```

Implementing types must use the interface's Prisma model or one of its inherited models.

`t.prismaField`, `t.prismaConnection`, `t.relation` and `t.relatedConnection` all accept an
interface ref as `type`. Fields on an implementing type can read the interface's `select`.
Implementing objects don't accept `isTypeOf`.

`resolveType` always has the row's `id`. If it needs other columns or to-one relations, add them
to the interface's `select`. To-many relations aren't available to it.

To add fields to the interface from another file, use `prismaInterfaceField` or
`prismaInterfaceFields`:

```ts
builder.prismaInterfaceField(Person, 'displayName', (t) =>
  t.string({
    select: ['firstName', 'lastName'],
    resolve: (person) => `${person.firstName} ${person.lastName}`,
  }),
);
```

To return rows through `Node` or another interface from a plain field, see
[Returning rows from other fields](./relations#returning-rows-from-other-fields).

An object type from `builder.objectRef` can implement a `prismaInterface` if its shape is
`PrismaPlanned` for the model, such as
`builder.objectRef<{ id: string; email: string; firstName: string } & PrismaPlanned<'User'>>`. The
shape must include the interface's `select` columns and the columns its fields expose.

## Native inheritance [#native-inheritance]

When Prisma itself defines inherited models, such as `Task`, `Bug` and `Feature`, the plugin can
choose the GraphQL type automatically. See [Model inheritance](./inheritance).


# Migrating from the Prisma plugin
URL: /docs/plugins/prisma-next/migrating-from-prisma
Updating an existing Pothos schema for Prisma ORM 8


Start with your Prisma ORM 8 client and contract, then update Pothos to use
`@pothos/plugin-prisma-next`. You can keep the structure of your GraphQL schema: `prismaObject`,
`t.expose*`, `t.relation`, nodes and connections still define the fields your clients use.

## Connect the new client [#connect-the-new-client]

Follow [Setup](./setup) to replace the plugin import, pass your contract as `PrismaContract`, and
configure `prisma: { client: db }`. The new client replaces the Prisma ORM 7 client and the
Pothos generator output used by `@pothos/plugin-prisma`. Use one plugin per program.

## What changed [#what-changed]

* `take` and `skip` are now `limit` and `offset`.
* `where` and `orderBy` use Prisma ORM 8's shapes, not Prisma Client's.
* The `dmmf`, `exposeDescriptions` and `onUnusedQuery` plugin options are gone.
* A `client` function also needs the base client's `context`. See
  [Plugin options](./setup#plugin-options).
* `prismaObject` and `prismaNode` take no `include` or `findUnique`. Use `select`.
* A connection helper's `getQuery` takes `(args, ctx)`, without `nestedSelection`.
* `@pothos/plugin-prisma-utils` has no counterpart.

## Declare data for computed fields [#declare-data-for-computed-fields]

Exposed fields and relations load their own data. If a custom resolver reads additional columns,
declare those with `select` so they are loaded whenever the field is requested:

```ts
builder.prismaObjectField('User', 'fullName', (t) =>
  t.string({
    select: ['firstName', 'lastName'],
    resolve: (user) => `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`,
  }),
);
```

Use a type-level `select` for data shared by every field or authorization check on that type.
[Selections](./objects#selections) covers both forms.

## Update queries and mutations [#update-queries-and-mutations]

For a read, `query` describes which rows to return. A field that previously spread the plugin's
query into `findUnique` can become:

```ts
builder.queryField('me', (t) =>
  t.prismaField({
    type: 'User',
    nullable: true,
    query: (_args, ctx) => ({ where: { id: ctx.userId } }),
  }),
);
```

If you already compose a native ORM query, return it from `collection`, for example
`collection: () => db.orm.Post.where({ published: 1 })` for published posts.
For writes, `resolve` receives the selected ORM query and lets you call `create`, `update`, or
`delete` on it. See [Mutations](./objects#mutations) for complete examples and
[Transactions](./transactions) for multi-step operations.

Custom `t.field` resolvers that return database rows should use
[`collectionFromInfo`](./relations#returning-rows-from-other-fields) when loading those rows.
This loads the relations and other data the GraphQL query selects.

## Keep your connection queries [#keep-your-connection-queries]

GraphQL clients can keep using `first`, `after`, `last` and `before`. In the schema, replace a
connection's `cursor` option with the order you want users to see:

```ts
builder.prismaObjectField('User', 'postsConnection', (t) =>
  t.relatedConnection('posts', {
    query: { orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' } },
  }),
);
```

The plugin adds a unique key to break ties. See [Ordering and cursors](./connections#ordering-and-cursors)
for nullable columns and supported sort fields. Root connections no longer take a `resolve` callback.
Use [`collection`](./connections#use-a-custom-collection) for checks before loading, and
[connection helpers](./connections#custom-connections) when a custom resolver needs the loaded rows.

## Adapt custom relation fields [#adapt-custom-relation-fields]

A filtered count now takes `query: { where }`, for example
`t.relationCount('posts', { query: { where: { published: 1 } } })`.

For a relation with custom resolver logic, use `t.field` with a `select`.
[`nestedSelection`](./indirect-relations) loads the relations requested beneath that field, and
takes its options in one object, such as `nestedSelection({ path: ['post'] })`.


# Objects
URL: /docs/plugins/prisma-next/objects
Defining GraphQL types backed by contract models


`builder.prismaObject` defines a GraphQL object type for a model in your contract.

## Define a type [#define-a-type]

Pass the model name and the usual object type options. Column types come from the contract.

```ts
builder.prismaObject('User', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    id: t.exposeID('id'),
    email: t.exposeString('email'),
  }),
});
```

The GraphQL type is named after the model. Pass `name` to call it something else.

To add fields to a type elsewhere, use [`prismaObjectFields`](#adding-fields). To expose the same
model as another GraphQL type, define a [`variant`](./variants) or a
[`prismaInterface`](./interfaces).
To return these objects from a query field, use `t.prismaField`; see
[Queries and selections](./queries).

## Selections [#selections]

Use `select` when a resolver needs columns or relations that the field doesn't expose. The plugin
loads them with the rest of the query:

```ts
builder.prismaObject('User', {
  // Loaded whenever a User is queried
  select: { firstName: true, lastName: true },
  fields: (t) => ({
    fullName: t.string({
      resolve: (user) => `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`,
    }),
    // Loaded only when emailDomain is queried
    emailDomain: t.string({
      select: ['email'],
      resolve: (user) => user.email.split('@')[1] ?? '',
    }),
    publishedPostCount: t.int({
      select: {
        posts: (posts) => ({ publishedCount: posts.where({ published: 1 }).count() }),
      },
      resolve: (user) => user.publishedCount,
    }),
  }),
});
```

A `select` accepts:

* Columns: `{ email: true }` or `['email']`.
* Relations: `{ posts: true }`, which loads the relation's scalar columns.
* Filtered or sorted relations: `{ posts: { where: { published: 1 }, orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }, limit: 5 } }`.
  `where` and `orderBy` take the same values as in `t.relation`'s `query`.
* A nested `select` for the relation's rows: `{ comments: { limit: 5, select: { post: true } } }`.
* `type`: a ref or model name for a [variant](./inheritance) of the related model. Only that
  variant's rows are loaded: `{ tasks: { type: Bug } }`.
* Counts and aggregates of a to-many relation, in a field's `select` only:
  `{ posts: (posts) => ({ postCount: posts.count() }) }`. Each key (`postCount`) is added to the
  row, so don't use the name of a column or relation.

A to-one relation only takes `type` and `select`. Aggregates have to be read in a resolver, because
`t.expose*` only works on columns.

A model's types (the object, its [variants](./variants) and [interfaces](./interfaces)) can each
have a `select`. If two of them select the same relation, they have to use the same options,
including in nested `select`s, or the schema build throws. `where` and `orderBy`
functions are compared by reference, so share one function between the types. To load a relation
with different options, use `t.relation` or a field's `select`.

To filter a to-one relation, select it and return `null` from the resolver. Here a comment shows its
post's title only when the post is published:

```ts
builder.prismaObject('Comment', {
  fields: (t) => ({
    postTitle: t.string({
      nullable: true,
      select: { post: true },
      resolve: (comment) => (comment.post.published ? comment.post.title : null),
    }),
  }),
});
```

### Selecting per request [#selecting-per-request]

A field's `select` can also be a function of its arguments and context. Here the field selects
`lastName` only when the client asks for the full name. A column that only some branches select is
optional on the parent:

```ts
name: t.string({
  args: { full: t.arg.boolean() },
  select: (args) => (args.full ? { firstName: true, lastName: true } : { firstName: true }),
  resolve: (user, args) =>
    args.full && user.lastName ? `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}` : user.firstName,
}),
```

With `AsyncSelections: true` in the builder's types, the function can be async.

The function's third argument, `nestedSelection`, is for custom fields that return objects. Use
it for a relation to load what the query selects under the field. The rows only include the
primary key and the selected columns, so pass it a `select` for anything else the resolver reads.
See [Indirect relations](./indirect-relations) for examples.

`select`, `query` and `where` functions are called while the plugin builds a query, not once per
row. They can be called more than once in a request, so they shouldn't have side effects.

### Resolver data [#resolver-data]

A resolver can read the model's primary or non-null unique key, the type's `select`, and its own
field's `select`. Other columns may not be loaded.

The type of a row loaded by the plugin includes `PrismaPlanned<'User'>`. To return rows from custom
resolvers, see
[Returning rows from other fields](./relations#returning-rows-from-other-fields).

### Auth checks [#auth-checks]

Auth checks on the type, and field options from other plugins such as `authScopes` and
`grantScopes`, can read:

* the primary key
* the columns and relations in the `select`s of the type and its interfaces
* on a `t.expose*` field, the exposed column

A field's own `select` is only available in `resolve`. If a row is missing any of these, the
plugin reloads it by its key before the check.

## Mutations [#mutations]

For a field that writes data, use `resolve`. Its first argument is the model's Collection, set up
to load what the GraphQL query selects. Filter it to the row you want to change, then call one of
Prisma's write methods:

```ts
builder.mutationType({
  fields: (t) => ({
    renameUser: t.prismaField({
      type: 'User',
      nullable: true,
      args: {
        id: t.arg.id({ required: true }),
        firstName: t.arg.string({ required: true }),
      },
      resolve: (users, _root, args) =>
        users.where({ id: String(args.id) }).update({ firstName: args.firstName }),
    }),
  }),
});
```

The mutation returns the updated row with the fields the client selected.

### Return a payload [#return-a-payload]

For a result shaped like `{ user: ... }`, use `collectionFromInfo` to load the fields requested on
`user`. The `path: ['user']` option tells it where that object appears in the result:

```ts
import { collectionFromInfo } from '@pothos/plugin-prisma-next';

const RenameUserPayload = builder
  .objectRef<{ user: typeof User.$inferType | null }>('RenameUserPayload')
  .implement({
```
